title: Lawmakers appreciate progress on effort to lower drug costs, but want to see more
summary: For the first time, a state board was able to tell lawmakers Thursday it is taking steps to bring prescription drug costs down for people on the state health insurance plan – a step more than five years in the making. But some lawmakers still have doubts.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 15, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters January 15, 2026

For the first time, a state board was able to report to lawmakers Thursday it is actively taking steps to bring prescription drug costs down for people on the state health insurance plan – a step that’s been over five years in the making.

But that progress wasn’t enough for several Republican members on the Senate Finance Committee, who continue to be skeptical about whether the Prescription Drug Affordability Board’s actions will actually result in lower out-of-pocket costs for Marylanders.

“That’s an issue that we’ve talked about over and over again in committee here — trying to address what is really the biggest consideration when you look at the cost of prescription drugs,” Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) said during the Thursday committee meeting.

His comments followed a committee briefing from PDAB Executive Director Andrew York, who reported that the board is gaining ground on cost reduction for two popular Type 2 diabetes drugs, but those actions are not finalized yet.

“For Farxiga and Jardiance, the board made their preliminary determination that these drugs cause affordability challenges and that then set the process for moving forward,” York said. “And then the final action is probably going to be occurring this spring.”

Formed by 2019 legislation, the board is tasked with bringing prescription drug costs down for Marylanders on the state’s health insurance plan. But various administrative hurdles and a lengthy rulemaking process delayed the board’s work for years.

Maryland board moves to set ceiling on what state will pay for Jardiance, Farxiga

In July 2025, the board selected its first list of prescription drugs to undergo a “cost review” process to determine if the six popular medications were unaffordable to Marylanders, with Farxiga and Jardiance the first to be determined “unaffordable” by the board.

But a longtime concern from opponents of the board, exemplified by Hershey’s comments, is that any cost-reduction efforts that result in saving taxpayer dollars may not result in lower out-of-pocket costs for patients.

“The real concern that we hear all the time is, ‘What are patients paying? What is their out-of-pocket expense?’” Hershey said. “There are some of us that say here that we could get through at the end of this and the patient might not see a penny of savings through the PDAB process.”

It’s not just Republicans who are antsy to see out-of-pocket costs come down.

Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) also expressed an interest in ensuring that patients themselves see savings. But he was appreciative of the progress made by the board this year.

“Given all these changes and whatnot, I’m glad to see that the board is now considering action for two of these,” he said.

York conceded that PDAB members have also indicated that the cost-review process is “kind of over-engineered,” and board staff will be looking for ways to streamline the evaluation process over the year to “tighten this process up.”

“We want to get it to an annual cycle,” York said.

Board members have an incentive to move quickly. Legislation from last session would expand the board’s authority out to all Marylanders, not just those on the state health plan.

But to do that, they first have to set what are called upper-payment limits under their current authority, which would mean the state places cap on what it’s willing to pay for those two drugs on the state health plan.

The board’s expanded authority would occur if it placed an upper payment limit on two prescription drugs for a whole year.
